name: PL-8177

card.summary: Experimental oral MC1r peptide in trials for ulcerative colitis; not studied for tanning or appearance.
card.note: Investigational; its studied purpose is inflammation, not pigment.

quick.overview:
PL-8177 is an experimental oral peptide that activates the melanocortin 1 receptor, the same receptor family linked to skin pigmentation.

Its published and registered research concerns inflammation, including a small ulcerative colitis trial.
quick.mechanism: It mimics alpha-MSH at MC1r, which in animal models reduced intestinal and ocular inflammation.
quick.risks: Not approved; human safety data are limited to early-phase trials.

lead: PL-8177 is an investigational oral peptide agonist of the melanocortin 1 receptor (MC1r).[1][2] MC1r is the receptor on pigment cells that sets skin and hair colour: when activated by alpha-MSH or similar ligands it shifts melanocytes from making yellow-red pheomelanin to brown-black eumelanin, which is why MC1r agonists such as afamelanotide and melanotan II are associated with darker, tanned skin.[3][4] This is the reason PL-8177 appears in discussions of pigmentation and tanning compounds.

The published development of PL-8177 has focused on inflammatory conditions rather than skin colour. Preclinical work with PL-8177 and a related compound, PL-8331, examined prevention and reversal of intestinal and ocular inflammation in animal models.[1] A phase 2a trial in active ulcerative colitis (n=16) began in September 2022.[2] No studies of PL-8177 for skin pigmentation or appearance have been published.

chain: MC1r activation is the receptor pathway that drives eumelanin production in other agonists
Potential pigmentation effects (not studied for PL-8177)
angle.text: Because it targets the same receptor that governs tanning and pigment type, PL-8177 is of interest to people following melanocortin compounds for skin tone. Its published research addresses inflammation, and no appearance study exists.

infobox: Ulcerative colitis; preclinical ocular and intestinal inflammation

paras: MC1r is a G protein-coupled receptor on melanocytes that raises intracellular cAMP when activated; its main natural activator is alpha-MSH, and agouti signalling peptide antagonises it.[3] Wikipedia lists afamelanotide and melanotan II among synthetic agonists, and describes loss-of-function MC1r variants as linked to red hair, fair skin and poor tanning.[3]

The 2018 preclinical paper describes alpha-MSH as having high affinity for MC1r and as preventing and reversing intestinal and ocular inflammation in animal models, and tested PL-8177 and PL-8331 to see whether they act similarly.[1] The work included an in vitro human whole-blood assay measuring inhibition of TNF-alpha, a rat model of bowel inflammation and a mouse model of uveitis.[1]

Afamelanotide (Scenesse) is a synthetic alpha-MSH analogue acting at MC1r. It began at the University of Arizona in the 1980s as a sunless tanning agent and is approved as an implant for adults with erythropoietic protoporphyria (EU 2015, US 2019).[4] Unlicensed melanotan products are sold online, and health agencies have warned against their use since 2007.[4]

NCT05466890 is a phase 2a study in active ulcerative colitis (n=16, active not recruiting).[2] A 2018 paper reported preclinical studies in animal models.[1] No studies found in pigmentation or cosmetic use.

timeline.event: Preclinical study of MC1r agonists PL-8177 and PL-8331 published.[1]
